section_summary: Pages 46–80 continue a 1946 issue of The New Taiwan Monthly devoted to Taiwan’s return to Chinese rule, its administration, population, economy, natural resources, Christian missions, and the chronology of the post-surrender takeover. Pages 81–90 concern the reported suppression in Japan of Sir Robert Clive’s letter advocating renewed British engagement, including a telegram, an internal note, and duplicate copies of a London Embassy despatch with the letter enclosed. Pages 91–99 contain a request to distribute World Youth in Japan, promotional enclosures, and the opening pages of its April 1948 issue.

subfiles.title: The New Taiwan Monthly: survey of postwar Taiwan
subfiles.from: The New Taiwan Publishing Co., Ltd.
subfiles.about: A promotional and statistical survey presents Taiwan’s history, people, resources, institutions, and first months under Chinese administration.
subfiles.summary: The issue describes Taiwan’s geography, Indigenous population, agriculture, forestry, sugar and fishing industries, governmental structure, and economic reconstruction following the Japanese surrender. It portrays Chen Yi’s administration as democratic and progressive while acknowledging food shortages, unemployment, communications problems, and dependence on retained Japanese technicians. Other material covers Christian missions, takeover personnel, government officials, the Cairo Conference, surrender ceremonies, and a detailed chronology from October 1945 through July 1946. Subscription and advertising forms conclude the issue.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1210 reporting censorship of Sir Robert Clive’s letter in Japan
subfiles.about: The telegram reports a Times story alleging that U.S. occupation censors prevented publication in Japan of Sir Robert Clive’s letter advocating renewed British involvement there.
subfiles.summary: The Times correspondent claimed that Japanese freedom of expression was becoming increasingly restricted by U.S. censorship. The immediate example was the rejection of Clive’s letter, which emphasized Japan’s former respect for Britain and the importance of restoring British interests. The telegram also notes severe censorial cuts to Lord Bryce’s Modern Democracies and the absence of Japanese editorial comment.

subfiles.title: Department of State note on the Clive-letter censorship incident
subfiles.about: An internal note summarizes the London despatch and questions the official explanation for initially blocking Clive’s letter.
subfiles.summary: The note records Mayhew’s statement that the letter was stopped because The Times lacked a formal license to distribute news in Japan, not because of its contents. It observes that the licensing problem was subsequently resolved and the letter published. The writer nevertheless suspects that the technical explanation may have concealed reluctance to allow the letter to appear.

subfiles.title: Despatch 4154, “Censoring of Article in Japan,” record copy and enclosure
subfiles.doc_type: Diplomatic despatch with newspaper enclosure and record-copy sheet
subfiles.from: American Embassy, London; Everett F. Drumright for the Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: The Embassy transmits Clive’s Times letter and reports the British parliamentary and Foreign Office response to its alleged censorship in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The despatch recounts Skeffington-Lodge’s House of Commons question and Mayhew’s explanation that the letter was delayed solely because The Times lacked a Japanese distribution license. Embassy contacts said the incident initially caused little concern at the Foreign Office, which sought a report from Tokyo only after the parliamentary question was announced. Clive’s enclosed letter urges Britain to revive educational and industrial involvement in Japan despite wartime atrocities and acknowledges the United States’ dominant postwar position.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Despatch 4154 and Clive enclosure
subfiles.from: American Embassy, London; Everett F. Drumright for the Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: A second filed copy repeats the Embassy’s report and the complete text of Sir Robert Clive’s letter.
subfiles.summary: This copy duplicates the account of the Commons question, Mayhew’s distribution-license explanation, and the Foreign Office’s limited initial reaction. The enclosed letter recalls Britain’s former prestige in Japan and argues for a mission of British educational and industrial experts. Clive recognizes American economic ascendancy but warns against Britain renouncing its Far Eastern interests.

subfiles.title: World Youth letter requesting guidance on circulation in Japan, with promotional circular
subfiles.from: Carolyn Smiley, Business Manager, World Youth
subfiles.to: Assistant Secretary of State, Department of State
subfiles.about: World Youth asks how it may distribute its nonpolitical educational magazine and solicit paid subscriptions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The business manager asks whether the magazine may enter Japan, whether paid subscriptions may be solicited, and whether a government fund purchases magazines for foreign distribution. Promotional pages advertise adventure stories about numerous countries and reproduce endorsements from educators. They describe World Youth as an independent, nonpolitical, nonreligious educational corporation owned by Maude Meagher and Carolyn Smiley.

subfiles.title: World Youth, April 1948 issue
subfiles.about: The opening of the April 1948 issue presents its contents and begins a Finland adventure story about postwar relief and reconstruction.
subfiles.summary: The contents advertise stories about Finland, India, science, Chichén Itzá, animals, and international friendship. The opening story follows Finnish-American relief worker Joe Mikkelsson along Finland’s Great Arctic Highway while he assists refugees displaced from territories ceded to Russia. It describes Rovaniemi’s destruction during the German retreat, Alvar Aalto’s reconstruction plans, and Joe’s journey toward Helsinki to arrange a shipment of food and clothing.
